one_liner: Multicore C++17 computational-geometry library (3D convex hull, kd-tree, spatial graphs) that outruns sequential CGAL and Qhull hulls through parallelism.
what_it_does: Research library from the MIT/UCR parallel-algorithms groups with parallel 2D/3D convex hull (pseudohull, divide-and-conquer, parallel quickhull, randomized incremental), a parallel kd-tree with k-NN, range search, bichromatic closest pair and well-separated pair decomposition, a batch-dynamic kd-tree, spatial graph generators (k-NN, 2D Delaunay, beta-skeleton/Gabriel, t-spanner, EMST), smallest enclosing ball, closest pair and Morton sort. The API is free template functions over parlay::slice/parlay::sequence of pargeo::point<dim> or fpoint<dim> (for example pargeo::hull3d::pseudo::compute(make_slice(P)) returns a sequence of triangular facets). It does not mimic CGAL or Qhull interfaces.
how_it_is_fast: All modules run on parlaylib's work-stealing fork-join scheduler. The 3D pseudohull first prunes interior points in parallel: it builds an extreme-point simplex, partitions points by the facet they see (split_k), recurses on each facet's points in parallel, then runs a parallel quickhull on the survivors; per search snippets of the paper, its parallel hull uses a reservation technique so several facets can be inserted into the hull concurrently. The divide-and-conquer hull splits the input into one block per processor, hulls each block with sequential quickhull, and hulls the union of block-hull vertices. The kd-tree splits in parallel during construction and runs queries data-parallel.
when_to_use: 3D convex hulls of millions of float or double points on a many-core machine (the paper used 36 cores with two-way hyper-threading), where single-threaded CGAL or Qhull is the bottleneck.
Batch k-NN or radius/box range queries over a static 2D-7D point set, where a parallel kd-tree build plus data-parallel queries fit the workload.
Building spatial graphs in parallel: k-NN graph, 2D Delaunay graph, beta-skeleton/Gabriel graph, WSPD-based t-spanner, Euclidean MST.
Research or prototyping that wants several parallel geometry primitives (enclosing ball, closest pair, Morton sort) on one scheduler.
when_not_to_use: Inputs needing robust hulls: visibility tests compare against a fixed absolute epsilon of 1e-5 in float/double (pargeo point eps, pseudohull numericKnob); there are no exact predicates in the code read, so very small, very large or degenerate (coplanar, duplicate) coordinates are risky, and the README says nothing about robustness.
Few cores or single-threaded builds: the claimed gains come from parallelism, and the repo's own benchmark compares only ParGeo's serial quickhull against its pseudohull, not CGAL or Qhull.
Hulls above 3D, or callers who need a half-edge/polyhedron mesh: hulls are 2D and 3D only, and the 3D result is a flat list of triangle facets (vertex coordinates).
Production code that needs maintenance: last commit 2022-09-12; the only issue (#1, January 2024, clang rejects a redefined default template argument in src/dataset/seedSpreader.cpp) is still open.
Dynamic kd-tree workloads where a maintained alternative exists (see Pkd-tree under siblings).

integration.form: static lib (each hull module builds its own CMake library, e.g. pseudoHull3dLib) plus header-only parts (kd-tree, point types)
integration.dependencies: parlaylib (ParAlg fork, pargeo branch, git submodule); batch-dynamic-kdtree submodule; Google Benchmark and Google Test for benchmarks/tests; pthreads
integration.min_toolchain: C++17, CMake 3.10; GCC-style flags; clang fails to build seedSpreader.cpp without the one-line fix in issue #1
integration.platforms: x86-64 as configured (CMakeLists hard-codes -mcx16 for 16-byte compare-and-swap); other architectures not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; parallelism uses parlaylib's global scheduler, whose thread count comes from the PARLAY_NUM_THREADS environment variable (default std::thread::hardware_concurrency)

gotchas: The root CMakeLists.txt overwrites CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS with set(...) (-DHOMEGROWN -pthread -mcx16 -O3 -DNDEBUG -fPIC), so flags you pass on the command line are discarded unless you edit it; USE_PARALLEL=OFF switches to -DPARLAY_SEQUENTIAL.
pseudo::compute is explicitly instantiated only for fpoint<3> and point<3>; other point types will not link without adding instantiations.
By construction the pseudohull filter only discards interior points, so inputs with most points on the hull (the repo's onSphere set) get little benefit from the pruning step.
The README's Multi-core Parallelism section is empty; thread control is only through parlaylib.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ParGeo over DGtal QuickHull (sequential, about 2x CGAL convex_hull_3) when you have many cores and very large 3D point sets and can accept epsilon-based float predicates; prefer DGtal for single-threaded or integer-lattice work. For parallel kd-trees, the Pkd-tree from the same research lineage (ucrparlay) is newer and benchmarks against the CGAL kd-tree and Boost R-tree directly, so use ParGeo's kd-tree mainly when you also want its WSPD, EMST or spatial-graph routines.
verified_claims_summary: Not reproduced, and the paper was not opened (arxiv.org, cs.ucr.edu, par.nsf.gov, dspace.mit.edu blocked). Search-result snippets of the ESA 2022 paper say the fastest parallel hulls on 36 cores with two-way hyper-threading are 10.5-124x (61.4x on average) faster than CGAL and 5.68-43.8x (19.9x on average) faster than Qhull for 3D hulls, while another snippet says pseudohull reaches up to 43.7x over Qhull and up to 5.05x over CGAL; the two statements conflict, and CPU model, compiler and CGAL/Qhull versions are unknown.
status_note: Abandoned since 2022-09-12 (one open build issue from 2024) but MIT-licensed; modules are small enough to vendor together with the parlaylib fork, and the ESA 2022 paper documents the algorithms.
